result.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers pick the same tiers with similar prices, explain why per-lesson and per-student pricing are worse, and work through the 40/45/15 split. A edges ahead because its migration plan is more concrete, its sensitivity table shows what happens if large studios leave, and it suggests specific checks: interview 8 to 10 large studios and watch the first 90 days. B is more explicit about the downsides of its own pick (teachers archiving students to stay under a cap, and the middle tier's 33% increase), but its guess at what a large studio earns is an unchecked assumption. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers recommend three per-teacher tiers at nearly the same prices, matched to the 40/45/15 split, and both explain why per-lesson and per-student pricing are worse. B is better on moving the existing 900 teachers over: it gives a dated announcement, a 3-month hold and a longer 6-month hold for large studios, while A offers alternatives without picking one. B is also clearer about what it doesn't know and how to test the prices: it suggests talking to 8 to 10 large studios, watching churn for 90 days with a set threshold for cutting the Large price, and running a churn sensitivity table. A names the downside of the tiers more directly, though: teachers archiving students to stay under a limit, and the risk of raising the middle tier by 33%.
